text: A remote backend tells Terraform to read and write terraform.tfstate against a shared storage service everyone on the team can reach, instead of a file sitting on one person's laptop disk. Configure it once, and every teammate who runs terraform init in that same project connects to the exact same state — no file to email around, and no risk of two divergent copies drifting apart.

A real azurerm backend block points at an Azure Storage Account you created ahead of time: resource_group_name and storage_account_name identify that account itself, container_name is the blob container inside it where state files actually live, and key is the specific blob name for this project's state file, so one Storage Account can safely hold many different projects' state side by side.

The s3 backend works the same way, just with AWS vocabulary instead: bucket is the S3 bucket you created ahead of time, ideally with versioning turned on so an accidentally overwritten state can still be recovered, key is the object path for this project within that bucket, and region is the AWS region the bucket lives in. Notice this block says nothing about locking yet — that's the dynamodb_table argument, and it's the whole subject of Lesson 11.

Once a backend block exists in your configuration, terraform init does more than just download providers — it also connects to that Storage Account or S3 bucket and confirms it can actually read and write there. Adding a backend to a project that already has local state from earlier lessons triggers a prompt asking whether to copy that existing state up to the new backend; answer yes, and nothing about your real infrastructure changes, only where its state record now lives.

From that point forward, the local terraform.tfstate file is no longer the source of truth at all, and it's safe to leave out of git entirely, exactly as it always should have been. Lesson 11 covers the one piece a remote backend alone still doesn't solve: stopping two people from running apply at the exact same moment against that same shared state.
